Former minister arrested in Paraguay’s latest Ueno Bank failure fallout

A former economy minister has been detained, accused of financial crimes linked to Paraguay’s collapsed Ueno Bank.

Paraguay’s former economy minister Carlos Fernandez Valdovinos has turned himself in to police.

On Friday, he became the latest former official placed under arrest following the collapse of one of the country’s largest banks.

The Ueno Bank crisis, which saw millions locked out of their life savings earlier this month, has already prompted the impeachment of President Santiago Pena, who has been arrested along with several other former top officials.

An arrest warrant for Valdovinos, seen by the AFP news agency, accused the 61-year-old of “alleged criminal acts of administration for personal gain, aggravated passive bribery, criminal association and money laundering”.

The public prosecutor’s office alleged that while he was minister in July last year, he approved the transfer of tens of millions of dollars in pension fund money to Ueno Bank.

He left office in August, after which he signed a multi-million-dollar consulting contract with the business group that controlled Ueno Bank.

Prosecutors believe the lucrative contract may have been linked to the pension fund transaction.

The Ueno Bank crisis

The crisis erupted on November 3, when Paraguay’s central bank took control of Ueno after declaring it insolvent.

In doing so, it froze account activity for nearly three million customers. In the months before its collapse, Ueno held roughly $850m in public funds, including money for retirement pensions. It left people struggling to access their savings, wages and pension payments, and raised questions about the government’s handling of public money.

The scandal led to the end of Pena’s presidency. A member of the conservative Colorado Party, a leading force in Paraguay’s politics, Pena saw his political allies distance themselves from him in the wake of the lender’s collapse.

His attempts to resign were rejected, as Paraguay’s Congress instead pursued impeachment proceedings. He was removed from office on November 6.

The bank had grown quickly under Pena’s presidency from a financial technology company into a large firm handling state pensions and the accounts of several government entities.

Pena is accused of using his position to direct millions in government funds to Ueno and concealing or downplaying its financial troubles, despite warnings of risky lending practices, while having financial ties to the bank. Pena has denied wrongdoing and said he sold his shares last year.

item.description:

Why it is here: Important cyberattack on a critical public service with clear reporting and useful context.

UK pensions department confirms cyberattack

November 28, 2026

The UK has confirmed a cyberattack on its welfare and pension systems, forcing several online services offline. Payments continue as normal, with no evidence so far that personal data was compromised.

The UK's Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has confirmed that a cyber incident that forced several online services offline was a deliberate attack.

The department said it detected an attempt to gain unauthorized access to its systems late Thursday. Several services, including online portals for state pensions, Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payment (PIP), were taken offline as a precaution. Some remained unavailable as of 5 p.m. local time (1700 GMT) on Saturday.

The DWP said in a statement on X that it was working with the UK's National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to "bring services back online as soon as possible" while investigating how the attackers had attempted to access its systems.

Officials said there was no evidence that personal information had been compromised.

Pension and welfare payments continued as normal despite the disruption to online services. The department also said it had immediately activated established contingency plans in response to the incident.

UK faces growing number of cyberattacks

The attack is the latest in a series of cyber incidents affecting British public institutions and businesses.

In recent years, cyberattacks have disrupted operations at the British Library, Transport for London and major retailers including Marks & Spencer, Jaguar Land Rover and the Co-op, according to Reuters and AFP.

Earlier this month, cyberattacks targeting software used by supermarkets across Europe disrupted operations at several UK meat suppliers. Fashion retailers Next and Asos have also separately reported incidents involving unauthorized access to data.

A cyberattack in August targeted three British airports belonging to the Manchester Airports Group, resulting in the theft of personal data of 8.7 million customers.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre warned earlier this month that the country should prepare for the possibility of AI-powered cyberattacks targeting critical national infrastructure in the next two years.

Downing Street said on Friday, November 27, that there was no evidence other government departments had been targeted in the cyberattack, according to DPA news agency. A government source told the agency that investigations into the attack and those responsible were ongoing.

The UK's Information Commissioner's Office, the data protection watchdog, said it was in contact with the DWP about the incident.

UK warns of Russian sabotage threats

The cyberattack comes amid a wider wave of disruptions affecting businesses and public institutions, including Microsoft and the US Federal Aviation Administration in recent weeks.

Separately, Britain's domestic intelligence service MI5 and the Ministry of Defence this week warned UK military suppliers to Ukraine about an increase in Russian sabotage attempts.

The government issued guidance on identifying and reporting suspicious activity and reducing the risk of attacks.

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

US civil rights group challenges ICE subpoenas as attack on speech

The ACLU lawsuit claims subpoenas violate First Amendment rights by targeting anonymous dissenters of ICE policies.

The Trump administration is abusing the grand jury process in an effort to unmask social media users anonymously criticising its immigration enforcement tactics, civil rights lawyers have claimed.

A federal class action filed on Friday, backed by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), seeks a court order enjoining the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security from conducting a “bad-faith investigation” that violates the anonymous individuals’ First Amendment free speech rights.

The scope of the investigation remains a mystery, but the ACLU says government lawyers have issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas seeking to identify critics and provide their personal information to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) investigators.

ACLU lawyers sued on behalf of four unnamed social media users, asking the district court in Washington to block subpoenas seeking account information for users of social media companies, including Meta, Bluesky and X, formerly known as Twitter. Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the ACLU case’s unsealing on Wednesday.

Boasberg scheduled a January 6 hearing for arguments on the ACLU’s request for a preliminary injunction against the government. The administration has until December 14 to respond in writing to the ACLU’s allegations.

Spokespeople for DHS and US Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office in Washington did not immediately respond to The Associated Press’s requests for comment. Pirro, Attorney General Todd Blanche and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin are named as defendants in the ACLU’s lawsuit.

ACLU lawyers say Pirro’s office has used the term “Investigation 18” to describe efforts to identify and obtain the personal information.

“The investigation,” the ACLU says, “is a bad-faith fishing expedition initiated to gather intrusive intelligence and facilitate retaliation against dissenters.”

The ACLU says its lawsuit in Washington is the “first systemic civil challenge, and the first case that will be litigated in public view, to the Trump administration’s abuse of grand jury unmasking subpoenas.”

“The government is weaponizing the grand jury process to retaliate against people for expressing their political views online,” Laura Moraff, staff lawyer with the ACLU, said in a statement. “The First Amendment guarantees our right to criticize the government, including anonymously, and no one should fear being investigated for disagreeing with the president. This crackdown on dissent is antithetical to our nation’s core values.”

The ACLU argues that the subpoenas to social media platforms are part of a broader pattern of intimidation. DHS has sent hundreds of administrative subpoenas to tech companies in the past year to seek information about online ICE critics, the ACLU says.

The civil rights organisation says the Trump administration has shifted to using grand jury subpoenas — a more secretive process — after encountering pushback to the administrative subpoenas from users and tech companies.

The ACLU lawsuit’s plaintiffs include a Bluesky user who wrote about an ICE-related shooting in New York by posting: “Burn ICE to the ground. Burn DHS to the ground. Salt the earth.” Another plaintiff is a college student whose posts on X included an expletive directed at DHS, ICE and Trump.

“Defendants’ rampant use of subpoenas to unmask critics of the federal government is occurring against the backdrop of repeated suggestions that Defendants are building a database of dissenters,” ACLU lawyers wrote.

Laura Follansbee, staff lawyer with the ACLU of DC, claimed the use of grand jury subpoenas was “an alarming abuse of power”.

“The use of subpoenas to punish social media users for their speech is chilling not only for our clients but for others who fear being targeted because of their political beliefs,” Follansbee said.

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-28 18:27 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: Argentina's bid to stop Falklands oil drilling rejected
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed report on a tragic event with clear reporting and useful context.

Argentina's bid to stop Falklands oil drilling rejected

Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.

The Argentinian government had called for the Sea Lion venture to be halted as it claimed there was an ongoing dispute over the sovereignty of the Falklands, a British overseas territory. The UK has repeatedly rejected that claim.

Speaking on Saturday, the president of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea said it was the wrong court to rule on questions of sovereignty. The decision was upheld in a vote 18-3.

After the ruling, Argentina's President Javier Milei said "this decision is not the final word" and declared "the Falkland Islands are Argentine".

Attorney General for England and Wales, Ellie Reeves, who presented the UK's legal arguments in Hamburg earlier this month, told the BBC the ruling was "really significant" and an "a clear win for the UK government".

Earlier, in a joint statement with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, Reeves urged Argentina to "end its wider economic pressure" against the territory: "Argentina sought to stop the Falkland Islanders making their own sovereign decisions and failed in this attempt."

The case is the latest diplomatic row between the UK and Argentina, which fought a 74-day war over the islands in 1982.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.

Two oil companies â Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum â are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.

But the Argentinian government claimed the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law, arguing that while it believed there was a territorial dispute over the Falklands, nothing should be done that could change the situation - including the building of oil wells.

The UK responded that the Law of the Sea court had no jurisdiction over the issue, and that pausing the Sea Lion project could have huge economic consequences on the islands' local population and companies connected with the venture.

The tribunal's decision ultimately rested on its own powers - this was a territorial issue, and a maritime court was not the right place to hear the dispute.

Buenos Aires disagreed, writing in a statement after the decision that "Argentina did not ask the court to rule on sovereignty", but to apply the United Nations' sea laws to the UK over its "exploitation of our resources".

It also said that five individuals would face sanctions for their involvement in the oil drilling venture, something Milei had been threatening. The statement did not specify who the sanctions would be against.

"The message is clear: those who participate in the illegal exploitation of our resources will face the consequences," the statement said.

Professor Marc Weller, from the Chatham House think tank, told the BBC Argentina's legal challenge had "provisionally, but spectacularly, fallen at its first hurdle".

"While this is only a ruling in a preliminary phase of the case which may be heard more fully by an arbitral tribunal next year, this outcome casts doubts on the viability of the Argentina's claim in those proceedings," he added.

The 10-week war that was fought in 1982 started when Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim over the islands, as a British military task force fought to eject them.

The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

Despite its defeat, Argentina has always maintained its right to the Falklands, and over the years, successive governments have pressed their claim with varying degrees of aggression and diplomacy.

The UK government has made clear that sovereignty remains with Britain and maintains that the island's population has a right to self-determination.

In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

item.title: Afghanistan: Several killed in blast near middle school
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important environmental issue with clear reporting and useful context.

Afghanistan: Several killed in blast near middle school

November 28, 2026

An explosion near a school in eastern Afghanistan has killed at least 10 students and injured 110 people. Officials say explosives at a nearby mining depot ignited due to negligence. An investigation is ongoing.

An explosion near a middle school in eastern Afghanistan's Kunar province on Saturday killed at least 10 students and injured 110 other people, most of them children, according to the Interior Ministry.

Authorities said a preliminary investigation indicated that the blast was caused by negligent storage of explosives at a depot near the school belonging to a mining company in the Andir Sir area of the provincial capital, Asadabad.

Deputy government spokesman Hamdullah Fitrat said initial findings pointed to "negligence and carelessness" at the depot. The explosion occurred at around 10 a.m. local time (05:30 a.m. UTC), according to earlier statements by provincial police officials.

Provincial officials warned that the number of casualties could increase. Unverified video footage posted on social media showed injured children being taken to the provincial hospital.

Samiulhaq Haqbayan, provincial director for information, told Germany's DPA news agency that the explosives were intended for use in mining operations and for clearing hazardous rocks from mountain slopes along the nearby Kunar-Nuristan highway.

Children among the injured

A school employee told AFP news agency that the explosion triggered panic among pupils.

"It was around 10 o'clock in the morning when an explosion erupted from that house, followed by screams of schoolchildren," said Latifullah, who declined to give his family name. "People scattered in every direction," he said.

An AFP journalist at a hospital in Asadabad reported injured children aged between eight and 15 being treated. Aliurahman, a local resident who helped transport victims to hospital, described seeing wounded children lying on the ground.

Abdullah, whose son was injured in the explosion, told AFP that the boy and his cousins had been trapped beneath a roof.

"My nephews are fine, but we took my son to the hospital, and thank God, he is doing better now," he said.

Third blast near a school this week

The ministry said an investigation into the incident is ongoing and further details will be announced once it is completed.

Saturday's incident is the third explosion near educational facilities in Afghanistan in the past week.

Two separate blasts near religious schools in Kapisa and Farah provinces killed a total of five students, with local officials attributing both incidents to unexploded ordinances left behind from previous conflicts.

item.title: EPA says initial tests show no toxic lead contamination in Iowa following detonation
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical report on a specific event with clear reporting and useful context.

EPA says initial tests show no toxic lead contamination in Iowa following detonation

Initial lab results from the controlled detonation of roughly five tons of unstable lead azide at a U.S. Army ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa showed no elevation of lead in water sources in the surrounding environment, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said Saturday.

"We will continue to provide updates in the coming days as new lab results for over 3,200 air, soil, dust and water samples (collected pre and post detonation) rapidly return and get validated," the agency wrote in a post on X.

The EPA says a team of 300 personnel and contractors spent the days immediately following Wednesday's blast collecting samples, in addition to monitoring for airborne lead for 30 consecutive hours.

Lead is a toxic heavy metal that does not degrade or break down over time. It's especially dangerous to children and pregnant people, and experts say there is no safe level of exposure.

Military explosives experts detonated 68 drums of aging lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown after it was found to be at risk of spontaneous explosion. Residents within five miles of the plant were ordered to evacuate, and many others told to stay inside, amid fears of a toxic plume of the chemicals.

In the hours immediately after the explosion, U.S. Army officials called the detonation a success, saying that the mitigation measures put in place – including layers of contaminant and downward-facing explosives meant to drive the blast into the ground – had "exceeded expectations."

Still, many residents and some elected officials have criticized the military for a lack of transparency in the operation, including Iowa Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand, who has called for an investigation into why the lead azide was allowed to get to this precarious point.

"The lead-up to the detonation should never have been so chaotic and unclear," he said after the detonation. "Iowans across the state are understandably alarmed and scared."

Sue Dyer, a corn and bean farmer about 18 miles southwest of the blast site, agreed that the biggest problem was communication, calling it "horrible."

"We didn't know anything about this until last week," she told NPR's Scott Simon in an interview on Saturday morning.

Dyer said that people in the community are all across the spectrum in terms of how worried they are after the detonation, even with reassurances from the federal government.

"Some people are sure that we're absolutely fine, and some people think we're absolutely dead. So put me somewhere in the middle until I have the data to make an opinion," she said, noting she is waiting for independent sampling results as well as those from the EPA.

Dyer says she had samples taken from her farmland before the blast and plans on taking her own samples again in the coming days, in hopes to get her farm verified lead-free.

"But what do you do if there's lead there?" Dyer asked. "I'm very hopeful that everything's fine, but I'm also a realist."

Source: NPR News | Published: 2026-11-28 17:32 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://www.npr.org/2026/11/28/nx-s1-6056359/epa-results-iowa-lead-testing

item.title: Argentina loses bid to stop Falklands oil project, vows to continue
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important international legal case with clear reporting and useful context.

Argentina loses bid to stop Falklands oil project

Argentina vowed to continue its efforts to stop the British-Israeli oil project off the coast of the Falkland Islands after an international court rejected its request for a temporary block.

The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) rejected on Saturday Argentina's bid to temporarily block oil drilling at the British-Israeli Sia Lion oil project off the UK-held Falkland Islands.

What did the judges rule?

At a special hearing in Hamburg, an independent court set up under UN auspices determined that Argentina's claims could not be resolved without first addressing the competing claims to sovereignty over the South Atlantic islands.

According to the judges, this question falls outside the scope of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that governs the world's oceans. Therefore, they rejected Argentina's claims by 18 votes to three.

The judges ruled that there was no reason to believe that the ITLOS had jurisdiction because it cannot make decisions based on questions of sovereignty.

However, Saturday's ruling was only preliminary, marking the start of what could be a long legal battle. The court urged both countries to swiftly establish the arbitration panel, which could still rule in Argentina's favor.

UK praises tribunal's ruling

"We welcome the decision by the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea not to prescribe provisional measures," United Kingdom Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Attorney General Ellie Reeves said in a joint statement.

"The UK has no doubt of our sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, our sovereignty and sovereign rights over the surrounding maritime areas, and the right of self-determination of the Falkland Islanders," they added, urging Argentina to end its wider economic pressure.

In a 2013 referendum, more than 99% of the approximately 3,500 islanders voted to remain part of the United Kingdom. However, Argentina rejects this result.

How did Argentina react?

Meanwhile, Argentina vowed to continue its efforts to halt a British-Israeli oil project near the Falkland Islands.

"This decision is not the final word," President Javier Milei said in a statement, adding that Argentina will continue to "assert its rights through all diplomatic, legal and administrative channels at its disposal."

Milei also vowed to continue punishing companies working on the oil project, calling it a "clear and present danger" to Argentina's claims over the islands.

Argentine-UK conflict over Falklands reignites

The dispute between Britain and Argentina over the planned drilling dates back to their 10-week war over the South Atlantic islands which have been under British rule since 1833.

In 1982, Argentina's military junta invaded the Falkland Islands (known as the Islas Malvinas in Argentina). The subsequent conflict resulted in the deaths of 649 Argentine troops, 255 British troops, and three islanders.

In 2013, the Falkland Islanders voted overwhelmingly in favor of remaining British. However, Argentina rejected the outcome. The country argues that the principle of self-determination does not apply to a population it considers to have been implanted by Britain after 1833.

item.description:

Why it is here: Detailed report on a tragic event with clear reporting and useful context.

Dozens killed in Myanmar military strikes on wedding venue and school

Air strikes by Myanmar's military have killed dozens of people across the South East Asian nation, including at a wedding venue and a school.

Rescuers said at least 21 were confirmed dead, and at least 35 others injured, at the wedding site in Moe Bye village, in the country's southern Shan state, on Saturday afternoon.

On Thursday at least 20 civilians were killed, including students, young monks and teachers, when an air strike hit a school at In Yon village, in central Myanmar's Magway region where resistance forces are active, according to Myanmar's exiled National Unity Government (NUG).

Myanmar's military-led government has not commented on the strikes.

The military also carried out air strikes in Mrauk-U town, in western Myanmar's Rakhine state, on Saturday evening.

At about 20:00 local time (13:30 GMT), a residential area in the town was bombed, reportedly killing more than 10 people and injuring about 20 others.

The area is controlled by the Arakan Army (AA) - one of the strongest ethnic armies fighting the country's military regime.

Military air strikes have been happening almost daily across the country since a coup in 2021 toppled the elected civilian government led by former leader Aung San Suu Kyi, resulting in a lengthy civil war.

Villages have been burned and ground offensives have been carried out by the military on areas it is unable to control, including territories controlled by the NUG and ethnic armed organisations.

The latest strikes come a week after Myanmar was found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

A 2017 military crackdown killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee, but Myanmar denied committing genocide - saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.

The verdict marked the first time a state had ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
